skill_title: Identify intermolecular forces and relate them to physical properties

items.question: What are intermolecular forces?
items.explanation: Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules, not within their covalent bonds.

items.question: Which intermolecular force is present in ALL molecules?
items.explanation: London (dispersion) forces occur between all molecules, polar or non-polar.

items.question: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is bonded directly to which atoms?
items.expectedAnswer: Nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine (N, O, F).
items.explanation: Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded to the highly electronegative N, O or F.
options: Nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine (N, O, F).

items.question: Which intermolecular force is the strongest?
items.explanation: Of the common intermolecular forces, hydrogen bonding is the strongest.

items.question: Stronger intermolecular forces lead to a... boiling point.
items.explanation: Stronger forces need more energy to separate molecules, raising the boiling point.

items.question: Which intermolecular force acts between polar molecules (in addition to London forces)?
items.explanation: Polar molecules attract via dipole-dipole forces as well as London forces.

items.question: When water boils, which forces are broken?
items.expectedAnswer: The intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules.
items.explanation: Boiling separates molecules by breaking intermolecular forces, not the covalent bonds.
options: The intermolecular forces (hydrogen bonds) between water molecules.
The O–H covalent bonds inside the molecules.
The bonds inside the oxygen atom.

items.question: Stronger intermolecular forces give a substance a... vapour pressure.
items.explanation: Stronger forces hold molecules in the liquid, so fewer escape — lower vapour pressure.

items.question: London forces become stronger as the molecule gets...
items.explanation: Bigger molecules with more electrons have stronger London (dispersion) forces.

items.question: Why does a non-polar molecule like methane still have some intermolecular forces?
items.explanation: All molecules, including non-polar ones, experience London forces.
options: It has no forces at all.

items.question: Why does water (H₂O) have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide (H₂S)?
items.expectedAnswer: Water has hydrogen bonding, which H₂S does not.
items.explanation: Water's hydrogen bonds (H bonded to O) are much stronger than H₂S's dipole-dipole forces, raising its boiling point.
options: Water has hydrogen bonding, which H₂S does not.

items.question: Why does HF have hydrogen bonding but HCl does not?
items.expectedAnswer: In HF, hydrogen is bonded to fluorine (N, O or F); chlorine is not in that group.
items.explanation: Hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F; chlorine does not qualify, so HCl has only dipole-dipole.
options: In HF, hydrogen is bonded to fluorine (N, O or F); chlorine is not in that group.

items.question: Two alkanes: butane (C₄H₁₀) and octane (C₈H₁₈). Which has the higher boiling point?
items.explanation: Octane is larger with more electrons, so stronger London forces and a higher boiling point.
options: They boil at the same temperature.

items.question: Why is ethanol more soluble in water than hexane is?
items.expectedAnswer: Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water; hexane cannot.
items.explanation: Ethanol's –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water, so it dissolves well, unlike non-polar hexane.
options: Hexane is more polar than ethanol.
Ethanol can form hydrogen bonds with water; hexane cannot.

items.question: Which substance has the LOWEST boiling point?
items.explanation: Helium has only very weak London forces, so it boils at a very low temperature.

items.question: A liquid that evaporates very quickly (high vapour pressure) most likely has...
items.explanation: Weak intermolecular forces let molecules escape easily, giving a high vapour pressure and fast evaporation.

items.question: Which list orders the intermolecular forces from weakest to strongest?
items.explanation: Typical strength order: London (weakest) < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding (strongest).

items.question: Ice floats on water because hydrogen bonds hold water molecules in an open structure. This shows intermolecular forces affect...
items.explanation: Hydrogen bonding gives ice a lower density than liquid water — an intermolecular-force effect on a physical property.
options: the number of atoms in water.

items.question: Why does a molecular substance generally have a lower melting point than an ionic substance?
items.expectedAnswer: Intermolecular forces are weaker than the ionic bonds in a lattice.
items.explanation: Weaker intermolecular forces (vs strong ionic bonds) mean lower melting points for molecular substances.
options: Intermolecular forces are weaker than the ionic bonds in a lattice.

items.question: Two molecules have similar sizes, but one is polar and one is non-polar. Which has the higher boiling point?
items.explanation: The polar molecule has dipole-dipole forces in addition to London forces, giving a higher boiling point.
